records.sourceFile: Sport-related Concussion Can be Prevented by Injury Prevention Program.pdf

paper.citation: Chen YL, Chou TY, Sung MC, Huang YL. Sport-related Concussion Can be Prevented by Injury Prevention Program: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Prospective, Controlled Studies. Sports Medicine - Open. 2025;11:136.
paper.abstract: Eight prospective controlled studies (2,571 athletes) were pooled to test whether injury prevention programs reduce sport-related concussion (SRC). Programs reduced the SRC incidence rate ratio to 0.66 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.85), and the effect did not differ by physical versus educational program type or by practice versus match exposure.
paper.tldr: Injury prevention programs were associated with a 34% lower rate of sport-related concussion across eight prospective controlled studies. The effect did not differ by program type or by practice versus match, but the evidence is mostly from male rugby, soccer and American football athletes.
paper.methods: Six databases were searched to March 2024 for prospective controlled studies of physical or educational programs aimed at preventing SRC; the review was pre-registered (CRD42022375416). Incidence rate ratios were pooled with a random-effects model, with moderator analyses for intervention type and exposure context, and study quality was rated with the NIH tool.
paper.findings: The pooled IRR was 0.66 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.85, p = .002) and heterogeneity was absent (Q = 9.29, I2 = 0). Physical training programs (six studies, eight data points; IRR 0.61, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.89) and educational programs (two studies, three data points, both Heads Up Football; IRR 0.76, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.30) did not differ significantly, and neither did match (IRR 0.67) and practice (IRR 0.71) contexts. Egger's test showed no publication bias (p = .97).
paper.limitations: Most studies were not randomized, five of eight did not state how SRC was diagnosed, and four of eight did not state whether analyses were intention-to-treat. Only one study included female athletes, and the authors advise caution in applying results to females. The Discussion calls the physical training reduction (IRR 0.61) not statistically significant and gives its CI as 0.41 to 0.89, but Table 5 gives 0.42 to 0.89, a range that does not include 1; the table values are reported here. The educational subgroup is two studies of one program in one sport, and the non-significant moderators do not show that the programs work equally well across types or contexts.
paper.practicalImplications: In male rugby, soccer and American football athletes, these results support including a prevention program as one part of concussion risk reduction. The review does not establish a protocol for female athletes, and the authors call for more prospective studies to develop one.
paper.athleteDev: Physical programs in the review combined strength, balance or dynamic stability, plyometric, landing and cutting, and neck strength work, usually in warm-ups. Balance or dynamic stability appeared in four of the six physical programs, which the authors describe as important to include. The review cannot show which component drives the effect.
paper.rtp: This review covers prevention before any concussion and does not measure symptoms, recovery or return-to-play decisions after one. It cannot guide return-to-play timing or clearance.
